name: Boston
info: Boston is a port city on the Shawmut Peninsula and Boston Harbor in Massachusetts, founded in 1630 by English Puritan settlers, a leading town of colonial New England and a centre of the American Revolution.

facts.founded: Founded in September 1630 by English Puritan settlers led by John Winthrop and Isaac Johnson, who crossed to the peninsula on the invitation of William Blaxton, its first European resident; the Massachusett people had lived and fished in the region long before.
facts.where: On the Shawmut Peninsula and the shores of Boston Harbor, an arm of Massachusetts Bay, at the mouth of the Charles River in eastern Massachusetts, United States.
facts.known: The Puritan settlement of 1630; Boston Latin School and Boston Common; the Boston Massacre of 1770 and the Boston Tea Party of 1773; the siege of 1775 and 1776; the abolitionist movement; the Boston Brahmins and the city’s literary life; the first subway in North America; land made from tidal flats
facts.today: Boston is the capital and most populous city of the state of Massachusetts.

t: Puritan settlers took up Blaxton’s invitation and settled the Shawmut Peninsula in September 1630, and Boston became the largest town in the Thirteen Colonies until Philadelphia outgrew it in the mid-18th century.
Resistance to British taxes and troops produced the Boston Massacre of 1770 and the Tea Party of 1773, and the siege that followed ended with the British evacuation on 17 March 1776.
In the 19th century the city became a manufacturing and financial centre, took in Irish and other immigrants, led the abolitionist movement and tripled its area with landfill between 1631 and 1890.
dyk: More than two-thirds of inner Boston’s modern land area did not exist when the city was founded: it was made by filling tidal areas, using earth from the levelled hills and gravel brought by train from Needham to fill the Back Bay.
ev: Puritan settlers cross to the Shawmut Peninsula and name the settlement Boston
The worst smallpox epidemic kills 844 people, and inoculation is tried for the first time in America
Members of the Sons of Liberty throw 342 chests of tea into the harbour in the Boston Tea Party
The British evacuate the city after the siege on 17 March
Boston is chartered as a city
The Great Boston Fire destroys about 65 acres of the downtown
The Central Artery/Tunnel Project, known as the Big Dig, is completed

sections.origins:
Boston stands on the Shawmut Peninsula, a rocky bulge joined to the mainland to the south by a narrow isthmus, Boston Neck, and surrounded by Boston Harbor and Back Bay, an estuary of the Charles River. Before European colonisation the region was inhabited by the Massachusett people, who lived in small seasonal communities along the Charles, which they knew as Quinobequin, “the meandering one”. They most likely moved between inland winter homes and summer communities on the coast, where the fishing shoals and shellfish beds of the tidal flats were used. The peninsula itself, ringed by mudflats and salt marshes, was more sparsely occupied than its surroundings. Excavations on Boylston Street have uncovered one of the oldest fish weirs in New England, which Native people built as early as 7,000 years before European arrival in the Western Hemisphere.

The first European to live on the peninsula was William Blaxton, an Anglican cleric educated at Cambridge. He arrived in 1623 as chaplain to an expedition that landed at Weymouth, and when that colony failed by 1625 he moved to the foot of what is now Beacon Hill, where he was entirely alone for more than five years. In September 1630 he wrote to Isaac Johnson, leader of the Puritan settlement at Charlestown, where the rockier ground lacked easily tappable wells, and offered the peninsula’s spring. The Puritans crossed that month. John Winthrop’s settlers found the peninsula nearly empty of Native people, most of whom had died of diseases brought by earlier settlers and traders.
sections.growth:
Johnson named the new settlement Boston after his hometown in Lincolnshire, from which he and the minister John Cotton had emigrated; the English town took its name from its patron saint, St Botolph. By 1633 the town had 4,000 citizens. Its harbour made it a port of shipping and fishing, a main stop on the Caribbean trade route that brought in molasses, and it was the largest town in the Thirteen Colonies until Philadelphia outgrew it in the mid-18th century. Its economy then stagnated, and by the middle of that century New York and Philadelphia were wealthier.

The Revolution and the blockades of the town and port caused a majority of the population to leave. From a base of 10,000 in 1780 the population approached 25,000 by 1800, and Boston was again one of the world’s wealthiest trading ports, exporting rum, fish, salt and tobacco. When it was chartered as a city in 1822 it had about 46,226 people. By the middle of the 19th century manufacturing had overtaken international trade, helped by the small rivers around the city, the Middlesex Canal and, by the 1850s, a dense network of railroads. Boston and New York became the financial centres of the United States, and Boston capital helped to fund the nationwide railroad. Between 1631 and 1890 the city tripled its area by filling marshes, mud flats and the gaps between wharves, and filled almost 600 acres of the Back Bay with gravel. The industrial base reached its height around 1950, and it declined as factories closed. The economy recovered after the 1970s with finance, education, medicine and high technology.
sections.rulers:
The settlement belonged to the Massachusetts Bay Colony, created by the Cambridge Agreement of 1629, whose first governor was John Winthrop. Blaxton’s grant of 50 acres, about a tenth of the peninsula, was bought back by the town in 1634, and the land became the town’s common, now the bulk of Boston Common. Town officials were chosen each year. In 1652 the General Court authorised the silversmith John Hull to mint the pine tree shilling, which the English government came to consider treasonous after 1661; the mint ran until 1682 and the coinage contributed to the revocation of the colony’s charter in 1684. Fearing that revocation, Boston’s leaders obtained a quitclaim to the peninsula in March 1684 from Josias Wampatuck, a descendant of the Massachusett sachem Chickatawbut. There is little evidence that Josias, Chickatawbut or their people ever lived on the peninsula, and the deed was backdated.

From 1686 to 1689 Boston belonged to the Dominion of New England, governed by Sir Edmund Andros for James II. He was overthrown in a brief revolt on 18 April 1689, and the Dominion was not re-established. In 1768 British troops occupied the town to enforce Crown authority, and from the siege of 1775 and 1776 the British garrison under Sir William Howe held it until the evacuation. The town became a city in 1822, with Josiah Quincy III as its second mayor, and it annexed neighbouring towns between 1804 and 1912, among them Roxbury, Dorchester, Charlestown and Hyde Park. By 1900 wealthy Irish Catholic political dynasties had taken political control of the city.
sections.life:
Early colonists believed that Boston had a special covenant with God, an idea captured in Winthrop’s “City upon a Hill”, and they legislated morality and enforced church attendance and education in the Word of God. Boston Latin School was founded in 1635. The Puritans exiled or punished dissenters: Anne Hutchinson and John Wheelwright were banished during the Antinomian Controversy of 1636 to 1638, the Baptist minister Obadiah Holmes was whipped in 1651, and Mary Dyer was hanged on Boston Common on 1 June 1660 for defying a law against Quakers. Boston’s first circulating library opened in 1756 with 1,200 volumes. Boston was also a prominent port of the Atlantic slave trade in New England, though Salem and Newport soon overtook it, and slavery was abolished in Massachusetts in 1783.

In the 19th century a financial elite known as the Boston Brahmins, a term coined in 1861 by Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., dominated society and became patrons of literature and the arts. Writers such as Emerson, Hawthorne and Longfellow wrote in Boston, and the Boston Public Library was founded in 1852 as the first free library in the United States. William Lloyd Garrison founded The Liberator there in 1831, and the city became a centre of abolitionism. Irish immigrants came especially after the Great Famine, and about 35,000 Irish lived in Boston by 1850. By the end of the century the core neighbourhoods were enclaves of immigrants: Italians in the North End, Irish in South Boston and Charlestown, and Russian Jews in the West End. The streets of the old town grew organically and form no planned grid.
sections.crises:
Six smallpox outbreaks struck between 1636 and 1698. In the worst epidemic, of 1721 and 1722, 5,889 of the town’s 10,500 people caught the disease and 844, or 14 per cent, died; at least 900 fled and spread the virus. Zabdiel Boylston and Cotton Mather introduced inoculation, tried for the first time in America and disputed, as it could be fatal to about 2 per cent of those treated. The earthquake of 1755 damaged buildings but killed no one, and the first Great Fire of 20 March 1760 destroyed 349 buildings.

Resistance to British measures led to riots against the Stamp Act in 1765 and to the occupation of 1768. On 5 March 1770 soldiers of the 29th Regiment fired into a crowd and five people were killed in the Boston Massacre. On 16 December 1773 members of the Sons of Liberty, disguised as Native Americans, threw 342 chests of tea into the harbour, and Parliament closed the port and removed the colony’s self-government. Patriot militia besieged the British from 19 April 1775 to 17 March 1776. The British won the Battle of Bunker Hill on 17 June 1775 at heavy cost, and they left after the Americans placed cannon on Dorchester Heights; two-thirds of the population left in the 1770s. A draft riot in the North End in 1863 caused 8 to 14 deaths. The Great Boston Fire of 9 November 1872 destroyed about 65 acres and 776 buildings. A flood of molasses killed 21 people in 1919, and the Cocoanut Grove fire of 28 November 1942 killed 492. Urban renewal from 1958 demolished the West End and Scollay Square, and desegregation busing brought riots from 1974 to 1976.
sections.legacy:
Boston is remembered chiefly for its part in the American Revolution. Evacuation Day, 17 March, is still celebrated there, and several sites of the period are kept in the Boston National Historical Park along the Freedom Trail. In the early 1800s William Tudor compared the city to Athens, and Boston came to be called the “Athens of America” for its literary culture. Boston Common, bought by the town in 1634, is the oldest public park in the United States, and the city’s firsts include Boston Latin School, the Boston Public Library and the Tremont Street Subway of 1897, the first subway in North America.

The shape of the old town is much changed. The three hills of the original peninsula, Copps Hill, Fort Hill and Trimountaine, from which Tremont Street takes its name, were levelled or lowered, and the State House stands on a shortened Beacon Hill. After the fire of 1872 building rubble was used as landfill on the waterfront. The Central Artery/Tunnel Project, the Big Dig, ran from 1991 to 2007, moved the elevated highway underground and made new green spaces.

Boston is today the capital and most populous city of Massachusetts. Its neighbourhoods include Back Bay, Beacon Hill, the North End and the South End, and it has a large number of hospitals and universities. Its people include descendants of Irish, Italian, African American, Caribbean and many other communities.

summary: Boston, on the Shawmut Peninsula in Massachusetts, was founded in 1630 by Puritan settlers on William Blaxton’s invitation. It was a leading town of colonial New England and a centre of the American Revolution, and it tripled its area with landfill. It is today the capital of Massachusetts.

Thomas H. O'Connor, Boston: A to Z (Harvard University Press, 2000)

notes: SPELLING: the city article writes Tremontaine, the history article Trimountaine; I used Trimountaine.

CONFLICT left out: the Boston Massacre soldiers are five in the city article and nine in the history article (I gave no number; five killed as the history article says). British troops sent in 1768 are 2,000 in one article and 4,000 in the other (no number given).
CONFLICT left out: population. The city article gives 675,647 (2020 census, lead) and 691,531 (Demographics) for the same census. No present-day figure is given in the text.

The history article says Boston was 'named and officially incorporated' on 30 September 1630 (Old Style); the city article says Johnson named it in one of his last acts before dying on 30 September 1630. I wrote only September 1630.
Boston Latin School 1635 and Harvard 1636: the history article calls them the first school and first college in America; I did not use Harvard (Cambridge).

Annexation dates: the two articles differ in detail (the city article lists East Boston 1836 and South Boston 1804; the history article lists Dorchester 1804 and Dorchester 1870). I wrote only the range 1804 to 1912.
The 'majority of the population' who fled and 'two-thirds' in the 1770s are both from the history article (one in the 19th-century growth section, one in its lead); I used both as given.
Founding: Blaxton’s years: the history article says he settled by 1625 and was alone for more than five years; 'by 1625' is my reading of 'by 1625 the colony at Weymouth had failed'.
Quitclaim of 1684: the article says there is little evidence that these Massachusett ever inhabited the peninsula; kept as the article’s attribution.
